guidance: Answer every initially active question plus each dependent question whose activation predicate is met by your earlier answers. Extra inactive branch answers are ignored and never committed. Preserve the approved Result target.

For each active question, review the inspected passages against its exact proposition and check material contradictions. Reuse adequate Evidence. When a premise remains unresolved, use bounded discovery across relevant Sources, including a protocol or SAP when relevant. Inspect returned passages before using them. A limitation requires a Trial-scoped, untruncated search receipt. Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

Cite complete premises for the active question. One passage may support several facts. When an answer depends on separate passages, cite each with its own boundaries. A relationship kind describes the use of Evidence; it adds no scientific fact.

When inference, conflict, or uncertainty connects Evidence to an answer, include a concise question-specific justification. State what the passages establish, what remains unresolved, and why the selected option follows. The server checks structure and Evidence identity; you judge whether the cited facts support the answer.
A definitive yes or no needs direct_support, indirect_support, or contradiction; a limitation or absence alone supports uncertainty, not a definitive answer.

Evaluate activation against your draft answers. If you cannot reliably resolve the complete active path, answer each question on that active path using an allowed official answer value and supported bases. Submit the complete active set in one validation call. The server commits only active answers.

Apply every reported repair and retain other drafted answers. Add missing questions to the existing answer set. Resolve further activation from the repaired answers before resubmitting. The server ignores inactive answers.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.

questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if a random component was used in the sequence generation process. Examples include computer-generated random numbers; reference to a random number table; coin tossing; shuffling cards or envelopes; throwing dice; or drawing lots. Answer ‘No’ if no random element was used in generating the allocation sequence or the sequence is predictable. Answer ‘No information’ if the only information about randomization methods is a statement that the study is randomized.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 17, Box 4, signalling question 1.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether a random component was used to generate the allocation sequence.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes when a random component was used; answer no when no random element was used or the sequence is predictable. A statement that the study is randomized alone supports no_information.
evidence_needed: The sequence-generation method, such as computer random numbers, a random number table, coin tossing, or minimization with a random element.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the only information about randomization methods is that the study is randomized. Do not turn missing reporting into proof that the sequence was non-random.

considerations: Minimization should generally be considered random when it includes a random element.

questions.wording: Was the allocation sequence concealed until participants were enrolled and assigned to interventions?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if the trial used any form of remote or centrally administered method to allocate interventions to participants, where the process of allocation is controlled by an external unit or organization, independent of the enrolment personnel. Answer ‘Yes’ if envelopes or drug containers were used appropriately. Answer ‘No’ if there is reason to suspect that the enrolling investigator or the participant had knowledge of the forthcoming allocation.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 17, Box 4, signalling question 1.2
questions.bias_construct: Whether the allocation sequence was concealed until participants were enrolled and assigned.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes for remote or centrally administered allocation independent of enrolment personnel, or appropriately used opaque sequentially numbered sealed envelopes or identical sequentially numbered drug containers. Answer no when the enrolling investigator or participant could know the forthcoming allocation.
evidence_needed: The method used before assignment and who controlled it; for envelopes or containers, capture the details that make them tamper-resistant and irreversible before assignment.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the report does not provide enough information to assess concealment; do not infer concealment from central registration or a sequence number alone.

answer_anchors.text: Remote or central allocation was controlled by an independent external unit, or appropriate envelopes/containers were used.
The enrolling investigator or participant had knowledge of the forthcoming allocation.

considerations: Allocation concealment concerns the process before assignment, not blinding after assignment.
The reported sequence-generation method does not establish concealment.
Use the returned query suggestions or wording from the report to locate the allocation safeguards. A truncated search does not establish that concealment details are absent.

questions.wording: Did baseline differences between intervention groups suggest a problem with the randomization process?
questions.official_guidance: Note that differences that are compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias. Answer ‘No’ if no imbalances are apparent or if any observed imbalances are compatible with chance. Answer ‘Yes’ if there are imbalances that indicate problems with the randomization process, including substantial differences between intervention group sizes, a substantial excess in statistically significant differences beyond that expected by chance, or imbalance in one or more key prognostic factors very unlikely to be due to chance. Answer ‘No information’ when there is no useful baseline information available.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance pp. 17-18, Box 4, signalling question 1.3
questions.bias_construct: Whether baseline differences between intervention groups suggest a problem with randomization.
questions.decision_rule: Answer no when no imbalance is apparent or observed differences are compatible with chance. Answer yes for substantial group-size differences, an excess of statistically significant baseline differences beyond chance, a key prognostic imbalance very unlikely due to chance and large enough to bias the estimate, or excessive similarity incompatible with chance.
evidence_needed: Baseline characteristics for the randomized groups, intended allocation ratio, prognostic factors, and outcome baseline measures.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when no useful baseline information is available, for example in an abstract or when only final-analysis participants are described.

answer_anchors.text: Baseline imbalance indicates a problem with the randomization process.
No imbalance is apparent or observed differences are compatible with chance.
No useful baseline information is available.

considerations: A few statistically significant differences at the conventional 0.05 threshold are usually compatible with chance.
This answer must not alter answers about sequence generation or concealment.
invalid_shortcuts: statistical significance of one isolated comparison

For patients receiving LHRH agonists, the use of
these agonists in combination with a first-gen-

randomization was recommended. First-genera-
tion antiandrogen therapy was discontinued be-
fore randomization.
Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio
to receive either darolutamide (at a dose of 600 mg
[two 300-mg tablets] twice daily with food) or
matched placebo. Randomization was stratified
according to the metastasis stage in the tumor-
node-metastasis system (nonregional lymph-node
metastases only [M1a], bone metastases with or
without lymph-node metastases [M1b], or vis-
ceral metastases with or without lymph-node or
bone metastases [M1c]) and according to wheth-
er the alkaline phosphatase level was below or at
or above the upper limit of the normal range.
Patients continued to receive darolutamide or
placebo until symptomatic disease progression,
a change in antineoplastic therapy, unacceptable
toxic effects, patient or physician decision, death,
or nonadherence.
End Points
The primary end point was overall survival,
which was defined as the time from randomiza-
tion until death from any cause. The secondary
end points were time to castration-resistant
prostate cancer, time to pain progression, symp-
tomatic skeletal event-free survival, time to a
first symptomatic skeletal event, time to initia-
tion of subsequent systemic antineoplastic ther-
apy, time to worsening of disease-related physi-
cal symptoms, time to initiation of opioid
treatment for 7 or more consecutive days, and
safety. Definitions of the secondary efficacy
end points are provided in the Supplementary
Appendix.
Assessments
During the trial, patients were evaluated every
12 weeks for evidence of castration resistance,
the initiation of subsequent antineoplastic ther-
apy, symptomatic skeletal events, opioid use for
7 or more consecutive days, pain progression,
the worsening of physical symptoms of disease,
and adverse events and serious adverse events
that occurred during treatment. Patients under-
went contrast-enhanced chest, abdomen, and pel-
vic CT or MRI and bone scanning at baseline,
within 30 days after the last cycle of docetaxel,
and yearly thereafter during trial treatment. Pain
was assessed with the use of the Brief Pain In-
ventory Short-Form questionnaire, and disease-
related physical symptoms were assessed with
the use of the Functional Assessment of Cancer
Therapy-Prostate (National Comprehensive Can-
cer Network) symptom index 17-item question-
naire. In safety assessments, adverse events were
graded with the use of the National Cancer In-
stitute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse
Events, version 4.03.
Statistical Analysis
The sample size was calculated on the basis of
the primary end point, overall survival. We esti-
mated that approximately 1300 patients would
be required to observe approximately 509 deaths,
allowing for a 5% dropout rate, which would
provide the trial with 90% power to detect a 25%
decrease in the risk of death in the darolutamide
group versus the placebo group, at a two-sided
alpha level of 0.05. The secondary end points
were tested with a hierarchical gatekeeping pro-
cedure in the order described above only if the
primary end point and each preceding secondary
end point in the hierarchy were statistically sig-
nificant. If the primary end point or a secondary
end point did not reach significance, the hierar-
chical procedure was stopped, and subsequent
analyses were considered to be exploratory.

BACKGROUND
Darolutamide is a potent androgen-receptor inhibitor that has been associated
with increased overall survival among patients with nonmetastatic, castration-
resistant prostate cancer. Whether a combination of darolutamide, androgen-
deprivation therapy, and docetaxel would increase survival among patients with
metastatic, hormone-sensitive prostate cancer is unknown.
METHODS
In this international, phase 3 trial, we randomly assigned patients with meta-
static, hormone-sensitive prostate cancer in a 1:1 ratio to receive darolutamide (at
a dose of 600 mg [two 300-mg tablets] twice daily) or matching placebo, both in
combination with androgen-deprivation therapy and docetaxel. The primary end
point was overall survival.
RESULTS
The primary analysis involved 1306 patients (651 in the darolutamide group and
655 in the placebo group); 86.1% of the patients had disease that was metastatic
at the time of the initial diagnosis. At the data cutoff date for the primary analysis
(October 25, 2021), the risk of death was significantly lower, by 32.5%, in the
darolutamide group than in the placebo group (hazard ratio 0.68; 95% confidence
interval, 0.57 to 0.80; P<0.001). Darolutamide was also associated with consistent
benefits with respect to the secondary end points and prespecified subgroups.
Adverse events were similar in the two groups, and the incidences of the most
common adverse events (occurring in ≥10% of the patients) were highest during
the overlapping docetaxel treatment period in both groups. The frequency of grade
3 or 4 adverse events was 66.1% in the darolutamide group and 63.5% in the pla-
cebo group; neutropenia was the most common grade 3 or 4 adverse event (in
33.7% and 34.2%, respectively).
CONCLUSIONS
In this trial involving patients with metastatic, hormone-sensitive prostate cancer,
overall survival was significantly longer with the combination of darolutamide,
androgen-deprivation therapy, and docetaxel than with placebo plus androgen-
deprivation therapy and docetaxel, and the addition of darolutamide led to improve-
ment in key secondary end points. The frequency of adverse events was similar in
the two groups. (Funded by Bayer and Orion Pharma; ARASENS ClinicalTrials.gov
number, NCT02799602.)

34|node-metastasis system (nonregional lymph-node
35|metastases only [M1a], bone metastases with or
36|without lymph-node metastases [M1b], or vis-
37|ceral metastases with or without lymph-node or
38|bone metastases [M1c]) and according to wheth-
39|er the alkaline phosphatase level was below or at
40|or above the upper limit of the normal range.
41|Patients continued to receive darolutamide or
42|placebo until symptomatic disease progression,
43|a change in antineoplastic therapy, unacceptable
44|toxic effects, patient or physician decision, death,
45|or nonadherence.
46|End Points
47|The primary end point was overall survival,
48|which was defined as the time from randomiza-
49|tion until death from any cause. The secondary
50|end points were time to castration-resistant
51|prostate cancer, time to pain progression, symp-
52|tomatic skeletal event-free survival, time to a
53|first symptomatic skeletal event, time to initia-
54|tion of subsequent systemic antineoplastic ther-
55|apy, time to worsening of disease-related physi-
56|cal symptoms, time to initiation of opioid
57|treatment for 7 or more consecutive days, and
58|safety. Definitions of the secondary efficacy
59|end points are provided in the Supplementary
60|Appendix.
61|Assessments
62|During the trial, patients were evaluated every
63|12 weeks for evidence of castration resistance,
64|the initiation of subsequent antineoplastic ther-
65|apy, symptomatic skeletal events, opioid use for
66|7 or more consecutive days, pain progression,
67|the worsening of physical symptoms of disease,
68|and adverse events and serious adverse events
69|that occurred during treatment. Patients under-
70|went contrast-enhanced chest, abdomen, and pel-
71|vic CT or MRI and bone scanning at baseline,
72|within 30 days after the last cycle of docetaxel,
73|and yearly thereafter during trial treatment. Pain
74|was assessed with the use of the Brief Pain In-
75|ventory Short-Form questionnaire, and disease-
76|related physical symptoms were assessed with
77|the use of the Functional Assessment of Cancer
78|Therapy-Prostate (National Comprehensive Can-
79|cer Network) symptom index 17-item question-
80|naire. In safety assessments, adverse events were
81|graded with the use of the National Cancer In-
82|stitute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse
83|Events, version 4.03.
84|Statistical Analysis
85|The sample size was calculated on the basis of
86|the primary end point, overall survival. We esti-
87|mated that approximately 1300 patients would
88|be required to observe approximately 509 deaths,
89|allowing for a 5% dropout rate, which would
90|provide the trial with 90% power to detect a 25%
91|decrease in the risk of death in the darolutamide
92|group versus the placebo group, at a two-sided
93|alpha level of 0.05. The secondary end points
94|were tested with a hierarchical gatekeeping pro-
95|cedure in the order described above only if the
96|primary end point and each preceding secondary
97|end point in the hierarchy were statistically sig-
98|nificant. If the primary end point or a secondary
99|end point did not reach significance, the hierar-
100|chical procedure was stopped, and subsequent
101|analyses were considered to be exploratory.
102|The full analysis set (all the patients who

4|underwent randomization and were assessed ac-
5|cording to the treatment to which they were as-
6|signed) was included in the analysis of the pri-
7|mary and secondary efficacy end points with the
8|use of a stratified log-rank test, with randomiza-
9|tion stratification factors. Hazard ratios for the
10|comparison of darolutamide with placebo and
11|95% confidence intervals were calculated with
12|the Cox proportional-hazards model stratified
13|according to the randomization factors. A log-
14|log survival plot, which was produced to assess
15|whether application of the Cox proportional-
16|hazards model was appropriate, confirmed that
17|the proportional-hazards assumption was met
18|for all time-to-event end points. Kaplan-Meier
19|estimates for overall survival are presented for
20|both treatment groups. For the analysis of over-
21|all survival, data on patients in whom death had
22|not been confirmed were censored as of the last
23|known date the patients were alive. For sub-
24|group analyses, intervals were not adjusted for
25|multiplicity and cannot be used to infer effects.
26|Descriptive statistics were used to summarize
27|baseline characteristics in the full analysis set,
28|and safety end points were assessed in the safety
29|analysis set (i.e., all the patients who received at
30|least one dose of darolutamide or placebo and
31|were assessed in accordance with the treatment
32|that they actually received). For the primary effi-
33|cacy end point, subgroup analyses were prespeci-
34|fied to assess the consistency of treatment ef-
35|fect. Statistical analyses were performed with the
36|use of SAS software, version 9.4 (SAS Institute).
37|Results
38|Patients
39|Between November 2016 and June 2018, a total
40|of 1306 patients underwent randomization at
41|286 centers in 23 countries. A total of 651 pa-
42|tients were assigned to receive darolutamide and
43|655 patients were assigned to receive placebo,
44|both in combination with androgen-deprivation
45|therapy and docetaxel (Fig. S1 and Table S1 in
46|the Supplementary Appendix). Of these patients,
47|1305 patients (651 in the darolutamide group
48|and 654 in the placebo group) were included in
49|the full analysis set, and 1302 patients (652 in
50|the darolutamide group and 650 in the placebo
51|group) were included in the safety analysis set.
52|Demographic and baseline characteristics
53|were well balanced in the two groups (Tables 1
54|and S2). The median age was 67 years in both
55|groups, most patients (71.1%) had an ECOG
56|performance-status score of 0, and 78.2% of the
57|patients had a Gleason score of 8 or greater
58|(scores range from 6 to 10, with higher scores
59|indicating a more aggressive form of prostate
60|cancer). All the patients had metastatic disease
61|at baseline; 79.5% had bone metastases (metas-
62|tasis stage M1b) and 17.5% had visceral me-
63|tastases (metastasis stage M1c). Most patients
64|(86.1%) had disease that was metastatic at the
65|time of the initial diagnosis.
66|At the data cutoff date for the primary analy-
67|sis (October 25, 2021), the median treatment
68|duration was longer in the darolutamide group
69|(41.0 months) than in the placebo group (16.7
70|months), and a higher percentage of patients in
71|the darolutamide group (45.9% [299 of 651 pa-
72|tients]) than in the placebo group (19.1% [125 of
73|654 patients]) were still receiving the assigned
74|trial treatment. Six cycles of docetaxel were
75|completed in 571 of 652 patients (87.6%) in the
76|darolutamide group and in 556 of 650 patients
77|(85.5%) in the placebo group. The reasons for
78|discontinuation of the trial agent are provided in
79|Figure S1. The median follow-up for overall sur-
80|vival was 43.7 months in the darolutamide group
81|and 42.4 months in the placebo group.
82|Primary End Point
83|The primary analysis of overall survival was per-
84|formed after 533 patients had died (229 patients
85|in the darolutamide group and 304 patients in
86|the placebo group). The risk of death was 32.5%
87|lower in the darolutamide group than in the
88|placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.68; 95% confi-
89|dence interval [CI], 0.57 to 0.80; P<0.001) (Fig. 1).
90|A significant improvement in overall survival was
91|observed despite a high percentage of patients
92|who received subsequent life-prolonging systemic
93|therapies, primarily different androgen-receptor
94|pathway inhibitors, among those who entered
95|follow-up in the placebo group (374 of 495 pa-
96|tients [75.6%]) (Table S3). The overall survival at
97|4 years was 62.7% (95% CI, 58.7 to 66.7) in the
98|darolutamide group and 50.4% (95% CI, 46.3 to
99|54.6) in the placebo group. The treatment effect
100|of darolutamide with respect to overall survival
101|was favorable across most subgroups (Figs. S2
102|and S3).
